proposition_text: American cities would be more affordable today if they had legalized denser housing two decades earlier.

proposition_text: Countries should phase out tobacco sales through a generational ban rather than rely only on conventional age restrictions.
reasoning: The decisive clash was CON's "proximity" mechanism: because legal supply remains open indefinitely while an ever-growing cohort of legally-barred adults lives, works, and socializes alongside legal buyers, proxy purchasing is uniquely easy and durable compared to a teenager's evasion problem under ordinary age laws. PRO's central rebuttal—that asking a spouse or friend for cigarettes creates meaningful "friction"—never squarely answered why that friction would hold for decades against a spouse or coworker with constant, casual access, especially once CON sharpened this in Rebuttal 2 and Closing with the "leak built into the design" framing. PRO's answers to the pressure questions (A1/A2) conceded diversion will happen but asserted, without much mechanism, that shrinking legal-buyer numbers outweigh growing barred-buyer numbers—this is asserted rather than demonstrated, and CON explicitly flagged this asymmetry (pool of buyers shrinks arithmetically slower than the pool of proxy-eligible relationships grows) without a real answer. CON also better weaponized the equality objection, converting it from an abstract complaint into a comparative burden ("proof of substantially greater prevention... PRO offers assumption, not proof"), which reframed the debate as a evidentiary weighing question that PRO's uncertain "our advantage is fewer initiations, not perfect abstinence" language could not satisfy. PRO's case was coherent and used the Q&A round reasonably, engaging directly with A1/A2 in proper format, which is a real strength, and its opening built a clear mechanism (permanent recruitment ban vs. temporary age gate). But across rebuttals, PRO increasingly conceded ground on diversion/proxy risk while asserting rather than proving that prevented initiation outweighs it, and never neutralized CON's "legitimacy cost" argument (spending ID-check credibility on carding 40-year-olds undermines the child-protection rationale that makes age laws work). CON's closing crystallized the clash cleanly and did not merely recap; PRO's closing also crystallized but rested on the same unresolved assumption. On balance, CON provided the sharper, more clearly won exchange on the decisive mechanism (durability of the barrier given proximity to legal buyers), giving it a clear but not overwhelming edge.
notable_rebuttals: CON's Rebuttal 2 response to PRO's "shrinking pool" framing—arguing that the pool of legally-barred adults expands relentlessly and lives in close proximity to legal buyers, making proxy purchasing a durable social favor rather than a fading friction—directly undercut PRO's central prevention mechanism and was never adequately rebutted.

proposition_text: Countries should phase out tobacco sales through a generational ban rather than rely only on conventional age restrictions.
reasoning: B built the clearer path to victory by making the live clash decide on structure, not slogans. PRO’s prevention story—prospective barrier, friction against initiation, grandfathering, seller-side enforcement—was coherent and stayed disciplined. But CON repeatedly forced the harder comparison: a dual adult market that keeps legal retail open for decades beside an expanding excluded cohort is a built-in proxy and diversion machine, not a shrinking problem that merely trims benefits. notable_rebuttals: B’s Rebuttal 1/2 turn that the legal-buyer pool’s contraction is outrun by expanding excluded adult demand living next to open lawful supply—creating lifelong arbitrage rather than genuine phaseout—most damaged A’s “contracting supplier pool = net prevention” route.

proposition_text: Countries should phase out tobacco sales through a generational ban rather than rely only on conventional age restrictions.

proposition_text: Countries should phase out tobacco sales through a generational ban rather than rely only on conventional age restrictions.

proposition_text: Countries should phase out tobacco sales through a generational ban rather than rely only on conventional age restrictions.

proposition_text: Countries should phase out tobacco sales through a generational ban rather than rely only on conventional age restrictions.

proposition_text: Museums and universities should return Indigenous and colonized peoples' human remains promptly even when researchers argue that continued scientific study would be valuable.
reasoning: Side B wins by maintaining a cleaner, more principled framework: legitimate authority over ancestral remains includes the power to refuse their use for research, and scientific value alone cannot justify overriding that refusal. Side A powerfully raised the asymmetry of irreversibility in the "last copy" argument, but never squarely answered who possesses the authority to override a community's present refusal on behalf of uncertain future beneficiaries. Side B absorbed that cost by noting that future descendants also inherit the consequences of denied community authority, and that institutions cannot assume their own priorities represent those descendants better than the community itself. Side B's distinction between identification necessary for return and separate scientific inquiry, combined with the decisive rebuttal that a time limit governs the duration of an override without justifying the override itself, left Side A's path to victory dependent on an unpersuasive institutional veto dressed in the language of archival preservation.
notable_rebuttals: Side B's sustained rebuttal that irreplaceability makes the request for consent more compelling but does not supply consent, and that a deadline limits the duration of an override without justifying the override itself. This exposed that Side A's "hard-stop" framework still negates the community's power to refuse and collapses into compulsory custody.

proposition_text: Museums and universities should return Indigenous and colonized peoples' human remains promptly even when researchers argue that continued scientific study would be valuable.

B's necessity-for-return distinction (ID enables return, disease study pursues separate benefit) and deadline-trap rebuttal left A needing to justify compulsory custody, while B could accommodate limited identification and voluntary partnership within "prompt" return.
notable_rebuttals: B4 answers to A3 plus the deadline-trap — if unread uniqueness justifies overriding now, why not again later? Forcing A to concede some irreplaceable loss is acceptable at its own deadline undermined A's absolute last-copy duty.

proposition_text: Museums and universities should return Indigenous and colonized peoples' human remains promptly even when researchers argue that continued scientific study would be valuable.

proposition_text: Museums and universities should return Indigenous and colonized peoples' human remains promptly even when researchers argue that continued scientific study would be valuable.

proposition_text: Museums and universities should return Indigenous and colonized peoples' human remains promptly even when researchers argue that continued scientific study would be valuable.

CON carved a procedurally safeguarded exception but conceded an independent order may keep remains over descendants' refusal — which B framed as "possession with a hearing" — undermining its own respect-for-agency claim and recreating the veto the proposition rejects.
notable_rebuttals: B's Q1/A1 exchange and B4-B5 crystallization that CON's time-limited, independently authorized hold that overrides a refusal is still a research veto — turning CON's honesty about overriding burial into the decisive liability.

proposition_text: Museums and universities should return Indigenous and colonized peoples' human remains promptly even when researchers argue that continued scientific study would be valuable.
reasoning: Side B successfully exposed the dogmatism of Side A's absolutist stance. notable_rebuttals: Side B's Rebuttal 2 and Closing, where they capitalized on Side A's explicit concession ("Immediate return even then") to show that Side A's framework disregards proven evidentiary necessity of the very abuse the proposition seeks to rectify.

proposition_text: The U.S. national debt has reached a level where serious deficit reduction should take priority over most new spending commitments.

proposition_text: The U.S. national debt has reached a level where serious deficit reduction should take priority over most new spending commitments.

notable_rebuttals: B's Rebuttal 2 bracket-quoting A's own concessions ([A4.1]-[A4.3]) to show that A's "documented assessment" process concedes exactly the litigation-gatekeeping problem B had warned about, turning A's attempted middle ground into evidence for B's slippery-slope critique.

proposition_text: Anti-encampment laws are justified only when cities provide genuinely available shelter, storage, and service options rather than simply criminalize visible poverty.
